nameStory: Eaton's Beggarticks gets its name from botanist Amos Eaton, a 19th-century professor who helped catalog New England's plants. The "beggarticks" part comes from the plant's notorious seeds, which have barbed tips that grab onto clothing and fur like tiny hitchhikers begging for a ride to new places.
description: Eaton's Beggarticks is a tall annual wildflower that can tower up to 5 feet high, making it one of the more imposing members of the sunflower family. Unlike many of its showy relatives, this plant produces small, understated yellow flower heads that usually lack the bright petals we expect from daisies and sunflowers. It's a coastal specialist that thrives in the salty, challenging conditions where land meets sea.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellow flower heads composed entirely of tiny disc florets packed together like a miniature sunflower center, usually without any surrounding petals (ray florets), though occasionally 1-3 short yellow rays may appear

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, upright annual that can reach 5 feet in height with multiple branching stems that feel sturdy and somewhat succulent to the touch

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Dark, wedge-shaped seeds topped with 2-4 barbed bristles that grab onto clothing with surprising tenacity when brushed against

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are arranged opposite each other on the stem and may be simple or divided, with a slightly thick, fleshy texture that helps the plant cope with salty conditions

habitat: Look for Eaton's Beggarticks along the edges of salt marshes, estuary banks, and other coastal wetlands where fresh and salt water mix. It thrives in the nutrient-rich, periodically flooded soils of these transitional zones. This is strictly a coastal plant in New England, so you won't find it inland.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin establishing their root systems in the salty marsh soils.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow rapidly, reaching their full impressive height and beginning to produce their small yellow flower heads in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Flowers mature and develop into the characteristic barbed seeds that will hitchhike on passing animals and people. Plants die back with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Only seeds remain, scattered in the marsh sediments waiting for spring warmth to germinate.

funFact: Eaton's Beggarticks is so rare in New England that it has been spotted only once in recent botanical surveys, making it one of the region's most elusive wildflowers and a true treasure for any lucky enough to encounter it.
confusionNotes: With 14 different beggarticks species in New England, telling them apart can be tricky! The key clues for Eaton's are its coastal salt marsh habitat and flowers that typically lack petals entirely. Most other beggarticks either grow in freshwater areas or have obvious yellow petals around their flower heads.
contextualKnowledge: Named after Amos Eaton (1776-1842), who founded the first school of science and engineering in the English-speaking world and wrote influential botanical guides that helped establish American botany as distinct from European traditions.
compareHints: Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils. While Devil's Beggarticks and Nodding Beggarticks are common throughout New England, Eaton's is restricted to coastal areas and typically lacks the showy yellow petals found on species like Smooth Beggarticks or Tickseed Sunflower.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
